overview:
Malta is a tiny island nation in the middle of the Mediterranean Sea, about 90 kilometers south of Sicily and 300 kilometers north of Libya. Its three inhabited islands, Malta, Gozo, and Comino, together cover just 316 square kilometers, smaller than many cities, yet more than 500,000 people live there, making Malta one of the most densely populated countries in the world. The capital, Valletta, is a fortified city of honey-colored limestone built by knights in the 1500s and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Maltese and English are the official languages. Maltese is unique: a language descended from Arabic, written in the Latin alphabet, and packed with Italian and English words, and it is the only Semitic language that is an official language of the European Union. Most Maltese are Roman Catholic, and the islands have more than 360 churches. Malta is a parliamentary republic that joined the EU in 2004 and uses the euro. Tourism, shipping, online gaming companies, and finance drive the economy, and the islands' harbors, beaches, and ancient temples draw millions of visitors.
landAndNature: Malta is a low, rocky plateau of limestone with no mountains, no rivers, and very few trees; the highest point, Ta' Dmejrek, is only 253 meters. The coast is dramatic, with sheer cliffs at Dingli, sea caves like the Blue Grotto, and sheltered bays with clear turquoise water perfect for snorkeling and diving among shipwrecks. Fields are divided by low rubble walls built over centuries, and prickly pear cactus and carob trees dot the countryside. Gozo is greener and quieter, and Comino has just a handful of residents and the famous Blue Lagoon. Summers are hot and dry, winters mild and rainy. Wildlife is small, from the Maltese wall lizard to migrating birds that rest on the islands in spring and fall, and the national plant is the Maltese rock-centaury.
peopleAndCulture: Maltese life revolves around village festas: each summer weekend a different town honors its patron saint with brass bands, streets draped in banners, and some of the noisiest fireworks in Europe. Food shows every influence that has touched the islands: pastizzi, flaky pastries filled with ricotta or peas, rabbit stew called fenek, ftira bread, and Sicilian-style sweets. Traditional wooden fishing boats called luzzu are painted in bright colors with eyes on the bow to ward off evil. Soccer is the favorite sport, and water polo is played in seaside pools all summer. Carnival in Valletta brings floats and costumes, and Good Friday processions are solemn and grand. Many Maltese speak three languages and switch between them mid-sentence.
history: Farmers built stone temples on Malta between 3600 and 2500 BC, including Ġgantija on Gozo, older than the pyramids and among the oldest free-standing buildings on Earth. Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Romans, Arabs, and Normans all ruled the islands; the Arabs left the language. In 1530 the Knights of St. John, a military religious order, took over and in 1565 withstood the Great Siege by a massive Ottoman army, then built Valletta. Napoleon seized Malta in 1798, and Britain took it in 1800. During World War II Malta was bombed relentlessly as a British base, and the whole population was awarded the George Cross for bravery. Malta became independent on September 21, 1964, a republic in 1974, and joined the European Union in 2004.
funFacts: Malta's Ġgantija temples were built around 3600 BC, more than a thousand years before Egypt's Great Pyramid.
The Maltese language is the only Semitic language written in the Latin alphabet and the only one official in the European Union.
Malta has about 365 churches, roughly one for every day of the year, on islands smaller than many cities.
The George Cross for bravery, awarded to all of Malta in 1942, appears on the country's flag.
Malta has no rivers or lakes, so much of its drinking water comes from plants that turn seawater fresh.
